questions.solution:
First law: mass deposited is proportional to charge passed, $w = ZQ$. Second law: masses deposited by the same charge are proportional to chemical equivalents $E = A/valency$.
Charge $Q = It = 2 \times 1800 = 3600\,\mathrm{C}$. Moles of electrons $= Q/F = 3600/96500 = 0.0373\,\mathrm{mol}$.
$M^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow M$, so moles of metal $= 0.0373/2 = 0.01865\,\mathrm{mol}$.
Atomic mass $= 2.22/0.01865 \approx 119\,\mathrm{g/mol}$ (tin).
questions.question: State Faraday's first and second laws of electrolysis. A current of $2\,\mathrm{A}$ passed for $30$ minutes deposits $2.22\,\mathrm{g}$ of a metal (valency 2). Calculate the metal's atomic mass. ($F = 96500\,\mathrm{C/mol}$)

questions.solution:
The more negative electrode oxidises: Zn is the anode, Cu the cathode.
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10\,\mathrm{V}$. A positive emf means the cell reaction $\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}$ is spontaneous.
questions.question: The standard reduction potentials are $E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}) = +0.34\,\mathrm{V}$ and $E^\circ(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}) = -0.76\,\mathrm{V}$. What is the standard emf of the Daniell cell $\mathrm{Zn|Zn^{2+}||Cu^{2+}|Cu}$, and which electrode is the anode?

questions.solution:
Nernst equation: $E = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{n}\log_{10}\frac{[\text{reduced}]}{[\text{oxidised}]}$ at $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
For $\mathrm{Zn^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Zn(s)}$: $E = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{2}\log\frac{1}{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}$.
With $[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}] = 0.01$: $E = -0.76 - 0.0295 \times \log(100) = -0.76 - 0.0295 \times 2 = -0.76 - 0.059 = -0.819\,\mathrm{V}$. Dilution makes the reduction potential more negative, as expected.
questions.question: Write the Nernst equation for a general reduction $M^{n+} + ne^- \rightarrow M$. Use it to calculate the electrode potential of a $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}$ electrode dipped in $0.01\,\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{ZnSO_4}$ at $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$. ($E^\circ = -0.76\,\mathrm{V}$)

questions.solution:
Rusting is an electrochemical cell on the iron surface. At anodic spots iron oxidises: $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$. Electrons flow through the metal to cathodic spots where oxygen is reduced: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$. $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ diffuse together and precipitate as $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_2}$, which oxidises further to hydrated ferric oxide $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$ (rust). Water with dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$/salts acts as the electrolyte.
Prevention: (1) Barrier methods — painting, oiling or galvanising (zinc coating) keep water and oxygen away from iron. (2) Sacrificial protection — connecting iron to a more reactive metal (Mg/Zn) makes iron the cathode of the cell so it cannot oxidise; the sacrificial metal corrodes instead.
questions.question: Explain rusting of iron in terms of electrochemistry (anodic and cathodic regions). Give two methods of preventing corrosion with the principle behind each.
